meta.title: Who really said "Deeds, not words"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: "Deeds, not words" was the 1903 motto of Emmeline Pankhurst's WSPU — but it's an old proverb she adopted, not a line she coined or is documented to have spoken.
meta.ogDescription: Emmeline Pankhurst made it the WSPU's militant motto in 1903 — but the phrase is the old Latin proverb 'res, non verba', not her coinage.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1858–1928 · British suffragette leader · founder of the WSPU
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely and correctly linked to Pankhurst as the militant motto of the Women’s Social and Political Union ↗, which she founded in 1903 — but it is an organisation’s rallying slogan, not a line she is documented to have authored, and the wording is a centuries‑old proverb she adopted rather than coined.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Latin res, non verba / facta non verba

trail: The WSPU ↗ was founded by Emmeline Pankhurst on 10 October 1903; its recorded motto is “Deeds, not words.”
The sourced quotations on Wikiquote ↗ — drawn from her 1914 memoir My Own Story — do not include this phrase, consistent with it being an organisational slogan rather than a personal quotation.
“Deeds, not words” is the plain English of the Latin proverb res, non verba ↗ (“deeds, not words”), a sentiment far older than the suffrage movement.
source.excerptNote: The WSPU’s motto — the phrase Pankhurst chose to signal a shift from petitioning to militant action. It is the English form of a long‑standing Latin proverb, not an original coinage.
source.rightsNote: As a three‑word proverbial phrase it carries no copyright in any case; adopted as the WSPU motto it dates to 1903 (before the 1931 U.S. cutoff), and the underlying Latin proverb res, non verba is ancient. It is firmly in the public domain.

author.name: Emmeline Pankhurst
author.heading: About Emmeline Pankhurst
author.metaLine: 1858–1928 · British suffragette leader · founder of the Women's Social and Political Union
author.bio: Emmeline Pankhurst (1858–1928) was the leading figure of the militant British women’s suffrage movement. In 1903 she founded the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU), whose members — the “suffragettes” — turned from petitions to direct action: marches, window‑breaking, hunger strikes and imprisonment. She adopted the terse slogan “Deeds, not words” to mark that deliberate break with decades of peaceful campaigning.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Pankhurst is real to this quote — but not the way memes claim. Two things get muddled.

items.why: “Deeds, not words” is the plain English of the Latin proverb res, non verba ↗ (also facta non verba), used as family and regimental mottoes long before 1903. Pankhurst adopted a ready‑made phrase; she did not invent it.

items.scope: What kind of quote it is
items.who: A WSPU motto, not a personal quotation
items.why: It was the organisation’s banner motto, not a line from a speech or book. Her sourced writings ↗, including My Own Story (1914), do not record her saying it as a personal statement.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: Pankhurst gave an ancient proverb its most famous modern life as the WSPU’s 1903 rallying cry ↗ — she chose it, she didn’t coin it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By 1903, women in Britain had petitioned peacefully for the vote for half a century with little to show for it. Emmeline Pankhurst’s answer was to break with that patience: the WSPU would be judged by action, not argument.

“Deeds, not words” captured that stance in three words — a proverb old enough to feel like common sense, wielded to justify marches, window‑breaking, hunger strikes and imprisonment. The slogan’s force came less from novelty than from who was saying it, and what they were willing to do.
context.pull: She chose an old proverb — and made it mean militancy.
